Disenfranchisement

/dis-en-FRAN-chyz-ment/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Disenfranchisement means the state of being deprived of a legal right, especially the right to vote.

In the 1890s, poll taxes across the American South achieved the deliberate disenfranchisement of Black voters, who could not cast a ballot without paying a fee many could never afford.

Worked Example

The lawsuit argued that purging thousands of names from the voter rolls weeks before the election amounted to the disenfranchisement of eligible citizens.

The sentence shows disenfranchisement as the taking away of an existing right — voters who were legally entitled to participate found that entitlement stripped from them.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

marginalization: Marginalization is the gradual pushing of a group to society's edges in many ways at once — ignored in media, passed over for jobs, unheard in politics. Disenfranchisement is one specific, formal blow: the removal of a legal right, above all the vote. Marginalization is diffuse; disenfranchisement is on the books.

exclusion: Exclusion is any shutting-out, formal or casual — from a meeting, a team, a conversation. Disenfranchisement is exclusion of one precise kind: carried out by stripping away a legal right, especially the right to vote. Every disenfranchisement excludes, but most exclusions take away no legal right at all.

disempowerment: Disempowerment is a general draining of power, confidence, or influence, by any means. Disenfranchisement is narrower and more official: the loss of a legally recognized right, above all the vote. A community can feel disempowered by neglect alone; disenfranchisement requires that some right actually be taken away.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

inclusion: Inclusion brings people into full participation rather than barring them from it.

empowerment: Empowerment builds up a person's power and standing instead of stripping it away.

Where it sits · how much freedom is stripped away — restriction → disenfranchisement → subjugation

restriction vs. disenfranchisement: A restriction merely limits how a right may be used, while disenfranchisement removes the right itself.

subjugation vs. disenfranchisement: Subjugation goes far beyond disenfranchisement, placing an entire people under domination rather than denying them one civic right.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dis-

Prefix — dis-: removal; reversal; undoing

Prefix — en-

Prefix — en-: to put into a state; to make

Root — -franchise-

Root — -franchise-: free; freedom

Suffix — -ment

Suffix — -ment: result or process of

Put it together

Put it together: This word is a whole sentence compressed into morphemes: en- + franc + -ment builds 'the process of being made free' — and then dis- slams into the front and reverses everything. Disenfranchisement is the undoing of that freedom: the removal of rights a person once held or was owed. The dis- prefix is doing all the destructive work; everything after it describes exactly what is being taken away.

Use the root in a new word: frank

Use the root in a new word: frank: Her frank reply held nothing back — the word comes from the same franc root, describing speech as free as the root's original meaning.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / civic-legal

Disenfranchisement belongs to legal, journalistic, and historical writing about voting rights. Do not confuse it with its near-identical opposite, enfranchisement — the only difference on the page is the prefix dis-, but it flips the meaning from granting a right to stripping it away.
